picks.title: 8 Stealth Taxes That Can Leave the IRS a Tip
picks.why: Taylor Schulte argues that your tax bracket understates what your next dollar of income really costs, because crossing certain income lines adds surtaxes, phases out deductions or raises Medicare premiums. He also makes the case that some of those lines are worth crossing on purpose. The useful takeaway is a simple three-scenario test to run before locking in year-end Roth conversions or gain harvesting. His audience is near Medicare age, so a few of the eight matter less for younger early retirees.

picks.show: Money For the Rest of Us
picks.search: Money For the Rest of Us
picks.title: Stock Pickers Keep Losing, Who's Winning?
picks.why: David Stein explains why active managers keep falling further behind even as their skill improves: index flows themselves push up the stocks that indexes already hold. He walks through research on who actually sells to index funds (mostly companies and insiders) and how much a dollar of passive flow moves prices, plus a San Francisco Fed paper on whether boomer retirement will drag on stocks. He closes with ways to own index funds without piling further into the S&P 500.

picks.title: Rob Arnott on the Hidden Costs of Passive Investing and the Real Winners From AI
picks.why: Rob Arnott argues that owning today's AI leaders is not the same as owning tomorrow's AI winners, and that cap-weighted index funds pay a real cost when stocks are added to the index, one that never shows up in the expense ratio. He makes the case for weighting by business size instead of market value. He also argues that GPU spending and depreciation are turning Big Tech into capital-heavy businesses, which matters for anyone whose index fund is now dominated by them.

picks.title: A Conversation With The Wealthy Barber
picks.why: Dave Chilton says most retirees get no advice at all on the order in which to draw down their accounts, and that tax-smart sequencing can be worth tens of thousands of dollars without adding any risk. He also pushes back on drawing tax-deferred accounts down early as a one-size-fits-all rule (Canada's "RRSP meltdown", a close cousin of the US Roth conversion ladder), and Ben Felix goes further, calling the blanket version irresponsible. It is Canada-specific in places, but the sequencing logic carries over.

picks.title: Dr. Daniel Crosby on Behaviorally Optimal Portfolios, Risk Composure and the Casino Myth
picks.why: Daniel Crosby argues that the best portfolio is the one you won't abandon, so he builds separate sleeves for safety, stability and growth instead of one optimized mix. He cites SEI research finding that clients holding a 6 to 24 month safety bucket were about ten times less likely to bail to cash in 2008, a behavioral case for cash buckets beyond the math. His stability sleeve is an unusual equal mix of large growth, small value, mid value, gold and intermediate Treasuries, and he splits risk into tolerance, capacity and "risk composure", meaning how likely panic is to override the other two.

picks.title: Q&A: I'm the Executor of Dad's $500K Portfolio. Should I Cash It Out?
picks.why: The bond question is the standout: a caller's long-term Treasury index fund fell 38% over six years, and the hosts argue that individual bonds take the same interest-rate loss even when no statement shows it. Joe Saul-Sehy calls short-term bonds a drag that barely keeps up with inflation and prefers T-bills for cash, while Paula Pant is buying 30-year Treasuries near 5.2% to 5.5% to hold to maturity. The hosts also disagree on whether an executor should move an inherited portfolio to cash during probate.

picks.title: AI Agents Are Already Changing the Price of Goods
picks.why: Lindsay Owens argues that pricing algorithms and AI shopping agents are ending the idea of a fixed price. In one test, 75% of 23 Instacart items were priced differently for different shoppers, with gaps of up to 23%, and AI agents told to find the cheapest option still steered users to pricier ones using their email and financial data. The episode doesn't discuss inflation statistics, but if prices become personal, the inflation a household actually lives through could drift from the CPI that inflation-linked bonds and withdrawal rules track.

picks.title: Episode 547: The RPR Reddit Forum, A Great Many Topics On Portfolios And Taxes, And Portfolio Reviews
picks.why: Frank Vasquez is the counterweight to the "Beyond Bonds" pitch below: he argues that covered call funds mostly change how payouts show up rather than total return, and that many new income ETFs are higher-fee packaging of old exposures. He also covers a listener rebuild of trend-following returns back to 1971 for backtesting managed futures, and the case for resetting withdrawal order and Roth conversions every year from tax brackets, health costs and income mix instead of following a fixed sequence. It leans on gold, so it's a good stress test if you don't.

picks.title: What If This Is the Worst Time to Retire?
picks.why: Ben Carlson and Christine Benz take on sequence-of-returns risk after a long bull market, and how today's higher yields change the withdrawal math. They cover buckets, front-loading spending, delaying Social Security and the case for a plain 60/40, and per the show notes they also weigh structured income products. It's a good check on whether an elaborate retirement income setup is doing more work than it needs to.

picks.title: AI Cyber Panic, Ken Griffin's Bubble Warning, The Fall of France?
picks.why: The first eight minutes are Ken Griffin saying AI is probably a bubble, and there's a long section on France's debt crisis. It's worth it for anyone uneasy about how much of a total-market fund now rides on AI, and for a bigger dose of sovereign debt stress than most FI shows give.

picks.title: #655 Vincent Deluard: The S&P Is Hiding a Bear Market
picks.why: Vincent Deluard, StoneX's director of global macro strategy and a longtime bull who has turned bearish, argues that a handful of megacaps are propping up the cap-weighted S&P 500 while most stocks are weak. He reads tax collections as a real-time gauge of the economy and argues Europe looks like Japan around 2012. The concentration argument is the part with lasting value; his closing trade ideas in the yen, the Korean won and UK stocks are tactical.

picks.title: Talk Your Book: Beyond Bonds in Retirement
picks.why: Calamos's Matt Kaufman makes the strongest pitch yet for replacing part of a retirement bond allocation with buffered, principal-protected, autocall and option-income ETFs, which he says now do what annuities and structured notes used to with clearer fees and ETF tax treatment. He cites roughly an 8.75% one-year cap on the S&P 500 with full principal protection. It's a sponsored segment, and a fully protected one-year product is essentially T-bills plus call options: nominal, with no inflation protection, and a cap that shrinks when rates fall. Pair it with Risk Parity Radio 547 for the rebuttal.

picks.title: What Wall Street Really Thinks About the AI Trade Now
picks.why: Barclays strategist Alexander Altmann argues the market is still in the denial stage of an AI boom, with stress showing first in cash-poor neocloud lenders and data center bonds, much as 2007 trouble started at the edges before reaching banks. He says the idea that AI spending is immune to higher interest rates is wrong, because heavy corporate bond issuance is now competing for limited capital even as rates stay high. He also expects most of next year's S&P 500 earnings growth to come from the AI ecosystem, which is a concrete way to see how much an index fund now rides on one theme.

picks.title: The S&P 500 Is Just 50 Stocks. The Nasdaq Is a 67% AI Bet. Kai Wu on What Else Is Hiding in Your Funds
picks.why: Sparkline Capital's Kai Wu looks through fund labels to show how the S&P 500, the Nasdaq, AI theme funds, emerging markets and even dividend and low-volatility funds can lean on the same companies and the same AI spending cycle. He argues that the number of holdings overstates diversification, and that cutting AI infrastructure exposure usually means loading up on the laggards instead, which is its own bet. Useful for anyone who owns several index funds and assumes they are spread out.

picks.title: J Scott Explains the Economic Domino Effect of an Energy Shock
picks.why: Investor and author J Scott walks through how an energy supply shock travels: oil futures move at once, gasoline follows within a week or two, and the effects work through supply chains into inflation and mortgage rates for months or years. He adds tariffs and deglobalization as extra pressure and asks whether the Federal Reserve can bring inflation down without stalling growth. A plain-language primer on the inflation channel that matters most to anyone living off a portfolio.

picks.title: Tech is Selling Off. AI Debt Fears Are Rising. So Why Does a $4B Manager See a Reverse Bubble?
picks.why: Money manager Jay Hatfield makes the bull case against the AI bubble story: much of the buildout runs on long-term compute contracts with investment-grade tenants, priced below today's spot rates, which makes it look more like contracted infrastructure than speculation. He pairs that with a rule of thumb linking the 10-year Treasury yield to the expected peak Fed funds rate and stock valuations, and explains why he avoids long Treasuries near 5%. Worth hearing for anyone uneasy about how much of a total market fund now rides on AI, because it is the strongest version of the other side.

picks.title: Anthropic S-1 Shocker, Greatest Business Ever? Google's $500B Wipeout, Midterm Predictions
picks.why: The hosts dig into Anthropic's IPO filing and its margins, and argue over whether Alphabet's post-earnings drop overshot. The part most relevant to long-horizon investors is the debate about AI borrowing: how much debt the buildout could add to bond markets, what that might do to Treasury yields, and how concentrated the economy has become in a handful of companies. The closing segment on the midterms can be skipped.

picks.title: 781. Ten Things I Do to Spend Peacefully
picks.why: Doc G, a retired physician, lays out ten habits that let him spend in retirement without second-guessing every purchase, set against ideas like Die With Zero. It treats the spending phase as a problem of anxiety and decision fatigue rather than of withdrawal-rate math, which is the part many careful savers find hardest after years of accumulating.

picks.title: Episode 548: The Intersection of Biased Skepticism, Shark Jumping (From Ep. 532), And Personal Finance Hoarding Culture
picks.why: Frank Vasquez responds to recent Early Retirement Now critiques of risk parity style portfolios, arguing that ERN's own toolbox gave a mix of US stocks, small cap value, Treasuries and gold a noticeably higher safe withdrawal rate than a classic 75/25 stock and bond mix, with the biggest gap at the worst historical starting points. He also argues that planning very long retirements to end with a large leftover balance amounts to hoarding, and that gold backtests using pre-1971 data mislead because gold was pegged to the dollar. It is one side of a public debate, but a sharp challenge to conservative withdrawal assumptions; the toolbox results come about 11 minutes in and the hoarding discussion near the end.

picks.title: Chip Stocks Look Cheap. AI Spending Is Surging. So Why Is Cameron Dawson Watching for Peak Earnings?
picks.why: NewEdge Wealth CIO Cameron Dawson looks at the AI chip trade from the earnings side rather than the valuation side. Her concern is that semiconductor profits could be near a cyclical peak, in which case today's modest price-to-earnings ratios are the classic trap of cyclical stocks looking cheapest at the top. A useful counterpoint to the more bullish AI cases going around, and a reminder to ask how durable the earnings behind a low multiple really are.

picks.search: The Psychology of Money Morgan Housel
picks.title: The Hardest Financial Skill
picks.why: Morgan Housel reads a short essay built on one of his best-known ideas, that the hardest financial skill is getting the goalpost to stop moving, then takes listener questions on returns from AI, how to think about bubbles, and making your younger self proud. A short, reflective listen on knowing when you have enough, which matters as much in the spending years as in the saving ones.

picks.title: Vanguard
picks.why: Ben Gilbert and David Rosenthal tell the full story of Vanguard, from John Bogle's firing at Wellington in 1974 and the unusual mutual ownership structure he built in response, through the rise of index funds, the ETF debate, 2008, Buffett's bet against hedge funds and the firm's first outside CEO. At close to four hours it is a long listen, but it is the best single account of how low-cost indexing went from a fringe idea to the default for millions of investors, and why Vanguard's structure lets it keep cutting fees.

picks.title: The $300 Billion Structured Notes Market Is Booming
picks.why: Nomura's Alex Micalizzi explains how structured notes pair a bank IOU with a derivative, why US sales are on pace for roughly $300 billion this year, and how they have become a popular way for individual investors to bet on AI. A clear look at how these products are built and priced, and at a large pool of AI exposure that sits outside the usual index funds and ETFs.

picks.title: Talk Your Book: Diversifying the AI Trade
picks.why: Nuveen's Brian Griggs talks through ways to own the AI buildout without piling further into mega-cap tech, from municipal bonds with high tax-equivalent yields to private money moving from data centers toward real assets and farmland, plus when to rebalance. It is a sponsored Talk Your Book episode, so treat it as a pitch, but it is a useful map of what diversifying away from the AI trade can look like.

picks.title: Seven Stocks Are 41% of the S&P | John Davi on Building Portfolios Beyond the Mag 7 Bet
picks.why: Astoria's John Davi, who builds ETF model portfolios, explains how he trimmed an equity overweight without calling a top and why he would move the classic 60/40 toward roughly 50% stocks, 30% bonds and 20% diversifiers such as real assets. He also suggests watching credit default swaps on the companies funding the AI buildout as an early warning sign, favoring AI adopters over AI builders, and using a quality screen to stay in growth stocks without riding the seven largest names. A practical take on what to do about index concentration rather than just worrying about it.

picks.title: The Liquidity Cycle Has Turned | Michael Howell on What It Means for Investors
picks.why: Michael Howell of CrossBorder Capital argues that the global liquidity cycle has turned, and that slowing liquidity can weigh on stocks even while AI earnings stay strong, because real-economy investment and a wall of maturing debt now compete with markets for the same funding. He measures liquidity as the financial system's capacity to fund rather than by the policy rate, walks through the four phases of his cycle and the role of bank reserves, repo, collateral and Treasury issuance, and makes a case for government bonds as liquidity tightens. He also touches on China's debt and what it could mean for gold. A useful macro lens that most retirement-focused shows never cover.

picks.title: Breaking Down Our Investment Portfolios
picks.why: Ben Felix and Dan Bortolotti open up their own portfolios and explain how they got there: Dan holds a simple 70/30 ETF mix, while Ben runs 100% equities with global diversification and factor tilts. They trace their views back to early influences, the 2008 crisis and research on wealth and happiness, and cover homeownership and cash reserves along the way. It opens with a physician describing how the show changed his approach to financial planning. A rare look at how two evidence-based advisors actually invest their own money, and why they ended up in different places.

picks.title: The Macro Implications of the Blue Tsunami
picks.why: Skanda Amarnath of Employ America joins Joe Weisenthal and Tracy Alloway to work through what this week's Democratic midterm gains could mean for the economy and markets: the future makeup of the Fed's rate-setting committee, the fight against inflation, tariffs, and the AI data center buildout. A fast, well-informed first read on the election's macro consequences while they are still fresh.

picks.title: Stocks Are Falling. The Economy Is Weakening. So Why Doesn't Mike Green See Passive Flows Turning?
picks.why: Mike Green of Tier1 Alpha makes his case that passive investing now shapes stock prices: steady retirement contributions flow through target date funds and market cap weighted indexes into the largest companies, while liquidity in those stocks doesn't grow with their market value. He explains how those flows may drive concentration and factor behavior, where valuation analysis still fits, and what could interrupt the buying, with employment trends the thing to watch. Useful for anyone who owns index funds and wants the strongest version of the critique of what passive flows do to the market.

picks.title: SocGen's Albert Edwards on 10% Yields and a 50% to 60% Drop | #656
picks.why: Societe Generale's long-standing bear Albert Edwards lays out why he thinks fiscal dominance could push central banks toward money printing, send the 10-year Treasury yield toward 10% and take the S&P 500 down 50% to 60%, with stocks and bonds falling together. He also covers China's weakening credit impulse, oil and food prices, what the IPO boom says about the cycle, and gold as a debasement hedge. An extreme view, but a clear one, and worth hearing as a stress test for any portfolio that counts on bonds to cushion a stock decline.

picks.title: Tech is Selling Off. Spending Is Outrunning Wages. What Happens When the Wealth Effect Fades?
picks.why: Bob Elliott of Unlimited and Aahan Menon of Prometheus Research argue that stock market gains are letting households spend faster than wages grow, and ask what happens to corporate profits if that wealth effect fades. They debate whether bonds look better than stocks or cash, how persistent inflation ties the Fed's hands, and whether AI is delivering the productivity and revenue gains outside tech needed to justify its investment boom. Both separate these risks from a 2008-style credit crisis, which makes it a measured counterpoint to the more dramatic bear cases.

picks.title: First Friday: Stocks Crashed. Jobs Boomed. Now What?
picks.why: The monthly economic roundup takes on a strange week: a record one-day loss in tech stocks, with the S&P 500 down 4.4% and the Nasdaq in correction, set against a jobs report that came in near three times expectations. It covers what concentration risk means for index fund investors when a sell-off starts in AI stocks, inflation running ahead of wage growth, a Fed hold with two members dissenting in favor of a hike, and a rule of thumb for where the 10-year Treasury tends to trade and what today's yield implies about inflation expectations. It also notes the 3.6% Social Security raise and the higher Medicare premiums that eat into it. One of the first calm walk-throughs of the sell-off.

picks.title: Jim Dahle: Is Avoiding Taxes Costing You Money?
picks.why: White Coat Investor founder Jim Dahle, who calls himself a recovering optimizer, talks with Morningstar's hosts about when cash, nominal bonds and TIPS each earn a place in a portfolio, how he thinks about direct indexing and tax-loss harvesting, and which strategies belong on the too-hard pile. The thread running through it is the case that chasing the last bit of tax savings can cost more than it saves. A useful check for anyone whose tax-efficiency rules have started to complicate their portfolio.

picks.title: Blue Wave Sell-Off. Four Market Pros on What Comes Next
picks.why: The show's monthly Last Call recap brings four quick interviews recorded after the post-election sell-off. Brent Kochuba of SpotGamma explains how options dealer positioning can amplify selling into November expiration; Ben Hunt argues the midterms clarified the limits of presidential power and handed governors more say over data center permits; Aahan Menon ties falling AI stocks to consumer spending through the wealth effect; and Eric Pachman tracks diesel and freight costs through producer prices to show how many industries face unusual cost increases, along with the Strategic Petroleum Reserve's emergency oil loans. Four different lenses on the same week, each in a few minutes.

picks.title: Episode 551: Stop Chasing Yield, The Limitations Of International Diversification, And Portfolio Reviews As Of November 6, 2026
picks.why: Frank Vasquez argues that autocallable, high-income and covered call funds mostly change how a payout is delivered rather than improving returns, and that forced income means forced taxes in a taxable account, so selling shares beats buying a built-in retirement paycheck. He then challenges global stock funds as largely a currency bet rather than real business diversification, suggests managed futures as a more deliberate currency tool, and makes the case that splitting value from growth protects better in a drawdown than splitting US from international. A sharp counterpoint to two very common portfolio habits.

picks.title: The AI Trade Is Cracking | Peter Boockvar on What to Own Instead
picks.why: Peter Boockvar of OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners explains how AI demand can keep growing while the companies building data centers still struggle to earn a return, using CoreWeave's multiyear lease commitments and borrowing costs as the case study, and traces how lenders, chipmakers and contractors each carry different risk if computing prices fall. He also reads the consumer through concerts, travel and hiring, covers oil inventories as shipping resumes and what Fed policy means for the cost of financing AI, and says where he sees value instead: overseas stocks, healthcare, consumer staples and gold miners. A clear map of where the stress in the AI buildout would show up first.

picks.title: Midterm Blood Bath, $4T AI Sell Off, Data Center Freeze, What's Next for Trump
picks.why: Much of the episode is election politics; the market-relevant discussion of data centers and AI comes later. The hosts argue that a state moratorium on new data center permits would push AI compute to Canada, Mexico, Southeast Asia and possibly the Gulf, raise the cost of compute, and favor the hyperscalers that already own their infrastructure. They also discuss how ending the war could bring oil prices down sharply and give the Fed room to cut, what AI regulation under a Democratic Congress might look like, and tax proposals including a higher capital gains rate on very large gains. A fast, opinionated read on how the election could reshape the AI trade.

picks.title: This $1.5 Trillion Manager Expects More Fed Hikes. So Why Is He Still Bullish?
picks.why: Mike Hunstad, president of Northern Trust Asset Management, estimates that AI now drives a bit over half of the risk in the S&P 500, yet he stays constructive into 2027 even while expecting further Fed hikes, pointing to tight credit spreads, contained inflation expectations and strong earnings growth. He calls AI the new beta, explains why equal weighting is not a real fix, and makes the case for a modest tilt toward quality, value and low-volatility stocks instead. He also argues the dot-com comparison breaks down because today's AI leaders generate enormous free cash flow, and warns that rising government debt could push up the term premium on long Treasuries. A clear framework for sizing AI exposure without betting the whole portfolio on it.

picks.title: The Perfect Storm That Clobbered Hedge Funds
picks.why: Bloomberg's Nishant Kumar, who covers hedge funds, and macro strategist Michael Ball explain why October was one of the worst stretches for hedge funds in recent memory and what they are watching after the midterms, from the AI buildout to the expected Anthropic IPO. It is a useful look at how professional money was positioned going into the AI selloff, which is the other side of the trade that index investors hold by default.

picks.title: The Winners and Losers of Index Investing
picks.why: Oxford's Martin Schmalz models indexing as a kind of tragedy of the commons: as diversification gets cheaper, demand for stocks rises, so each buyer pays more and expects to earn less, while more risk-averse bond holders come out ahead. He also walks through the evidence linking common ownership of competing firms to higher consumer prices, using airline routes as the case study, though he notes this is driven less by index funds than by large concentrated owners and centralized voting. The second half covers why wealthy investors so often avoid low-cost diversified portfolios, how fees compound over a generation, and family office governance. The practical takeaway is to plan around lower expected equity returns, even though individual index investors have little to worry about.

picks.title: What Nvidia's Megaspeed Scandal Is Really All About
picks.why: Bloomberg's Mackenzie Hawkins explains Megaspeed, a Singapore cloud company that has bought large numbers of Nvidia chips, how advanced chips get smuggled around export rules, and where the Washington fight over export controls now stands. Megaspeed denies wrongdoing and Nvidia says it found no evidence of smuggling. Worth a listen as a policy risk aimed at the biggest company in the major US stock indexes.

picks.title: We Haven't Seen This in 100 Years | Jim Paulsen on What Could End Tech's 20-Year Run
picks.why: Jim Paulsen splits the economy in two: a fast-growing tech, software and intellectual property slice of roughly 14% of GDP, and an old economy making up the rest that is growing at close to a recession pace. He argues that tech's leadership run, now about 20 years, is the longest he can find in roughly a century, compared with past runs of four to eight years, and that the real risk is complacency rather than exuberance. He expects new era stocks could fall 20% to 30% in a downturn while old economy sectors hold up, leaving the broad index with only a mild correction, and he warns that stocks and bonds have started moving together again. He also calls current inflation supply driven, so tightening to fight it would be a double mistake. A strong contrarian case for looking at what cap-weighted index funds underweight.

picks.title: RenMac's Jeff deGraaf: There Is Finally an Alternative to Stocks | #657
picks.why: Technical analyst Jeff deGraaf of Renaissance Macro argues that real yields above 2% have made bonds a credible alternative to stocks again, offering meaningful return with less volatility. He describes how bubbles grow when markets turn one-dimensional and everyone chases the same story, and makes the case for riding the trend while preparing for a reversal rather than fighting it. He uses semiconductors as a gauge of bubble risk, walks through how he reads the tape to spot regime shifts, and closes on credit: spreads, strain in lower-quality corporate debt, and deterioration in private credit that may be tightening financial conditions before it shows up in the wider economy.

picks.title: Episode 552: Using Margin Accounts For Cash Management, Canadian Funds, And A Deep Dive On Principles Of Valuation As Applied To Gold
picks.why: Frank Vasquez explains using a brokerage margin account as a short-term cash and tax-timing tool in retirement: covering a lumpy expense or bridging a few months to push taxable events into the next year, then repaying, instead of holding a large cash pile in a taxable account. He covers Canadian-listed options for gold, managed futures and US Treasuries, flags a methodology change at the CTA fund, and then takes on the claim that gold is pure speculation because it has no cash flow. His rebuttal: cash flow and expected return are different things, discounted cash flow is only one valuation method among several, and gold earns its place by its role as a diversifier that has historically supported higher safe withdrawal rates.

picks.title: Stock Investors Fear an AI Bubble. Bond Investors Fear Inflation. How Can You Diversify Without Selling Them?
picks.why: Corey Hoffstein and Adam Butler, joined by Matt Zeigler, make the case for return stacking: keeping full stock and bond exposure and using futures leverage to layer a diversifier such as managed futures on top, instead of selling stocks or bonds to make room. Their starting point is that inflation can hit both halves of a 60/40 portfolio at once. They explain why a zero-correlation strategy is not crash protection and can lose money on the same day stocks fall, why investors so often abandon diversifiers during long drawdowns, and what the 2008 portable alpha and hedge fund liquidity failures teach about leverage and collateral. They also discuss which risks are worth adding with leverage, the long-run record of managed futures, and an argument that investors drawing down a portfolio should lean toward trend following.

picks.title: Fidelity's Jurrien Timmer on AI Spending, Bond Yields and the Next Phase of the Bull Market
picks.why: Fidelity's Jurrien Timmer explains how to tell a rate-driven stock selloff from a growth scare: they look alike in stocks but do opposite things to bonds, which decides whether bonds cushion the drop. He walks through his investment clock, the Fed model of stocks versus bonds, the case for bond income, and a 60/20/20 portfolio with a fifth in gold and commodities. He also covers AI data-center spending and its financing limits, companies shifting cash from buybacks to capital spending, semiconductor earnings near a cyclical peak just as valuations look cheapest, real yields and fiscal risk, lessons from 1994 and 1999, and rebalancing when others are selling.

picks.title: How Wall Street Is Bracing For the Post-Jensen Huang Nvidia Era
picks.why: Bernstein's Stacy Rasgon explains why he downgraded Nvidia after Jensen Huang's resignation and why he is pessimistic about the stock in the near term. He covers key-person risk, who the board might pick as the next CEO, the risk of a government crackdown on the company's business practices in Asia and the Washington fight over chip exports to China, and whether customers now shift toward AMD and Broadcom. Two details stand out: Nvidia changed its revenue reporting to count sales by where the customer is based rather than where chips ship, which can obscure deliveries routed through Singapore and Malaysia, and its heavy supply chain financing is a risk of its own. He also says what he is watching going into Nvidia's earnings and whether the uncertainty spreads to AI labs and data center providers.

picks.title: 9 Retirement Mistakes You May Not Be Able to Undo
picks.why: Taylor Schulte walks through nine retirement decisions that are hard or impossible to reverse, roughly in the order retirees meet them. They include rolling appreciated company stock into an IRA without checking net unrealized appreciation, losing the age 55 rule by rolling a 401(k) into an IRA, taking a rollover check made payable to the account owner and the 20% withholding that follows, picking a single-life pension with no survivor benefit, the one-time Social Security withdrawal and voluntary suspension, the Medicare Part B penalty and the eight-month window after employer coverage, and HSA contributions that become excess once Medicare Part A is backdated up to six months. On taxes, federal tax withheld from an IRA distribution counts as paid evenly through the year, so a December withholding can cure an estimated tax shortfall where a December estimated payment cannot. The last mistake is trusting a will or divorce decree over a beneficiary form, illustrated by the 2009 Supreme Court case Kennedy v. DuPont, where about $400,000 went to an ex-spouse named on an old form.

picks.title: Stocks Are Falling. Put Buying Hit a Record. So Why Does an Options Trader See a Thanksgiving Rally?
picks.why: Brent Kochuba of SpotGamma reads the options market after a record day for S&P 500 put buying on November 5. He explains how dealer hedging and options expiration move prices, why the market is in a negative gamma regime that amplifies swings, and which index levels he sees as resistance and support. His base case is that volatility drains once this week's catalysts pass (Nvidia earnings, VIX expiration, the Anthropic IPO and November options expiration), setting up a rally into Thanksgiving, though he is less sure about December. He calls a December Fed hike nearly certain with the 10-year yield back near 5%, and argues that rising rates broke the rotation from tech into rate-sensitive sectors that had been supporting the market. He treats the neocloud stocks as the signal for whether any tech rally can hold. It is a trader's view of one specific week, so it is most useful heard soon.

picks.title: Are You Taking More Investment Risk Than Your Goals Require? | With Brandon Bouier (Ep. 115)
picks.why: Steve Chen talks with Brandon Bouier, founder of the Day Two Investing community, which grew out of personal finance conversations among Amazon employees after Bouier moved from government work into big tech. The core of the hour is concentration risk from employer stock and stock-based compensation, which ties a career and a portfolio to the same company, and the case for taking only as much investment risk as a goal actually requires by working backward from the goal. They also cover the cost of playing it too safe, investor behavior and dollar-cost averaging through downturns, how AI and data center spending are changing tech careers, and where AI tools fit next to a financial advisor. It is not tied to the news, so it keeps.

picks.title: The Impossible Trilemma That Hangs Over the Nvidia Crisis
picks.why: Tian Yang of Variant Perception argues that a government cannot pay for defense and industrial buildout, entitlements and low inflation all at once, and that history shows low inflation is the one that gives way. He expects financial repression, roughly 4 to 5% inflation while rates are held down, along with tools like stablecoins as captive Treasury buyers, bill-heavy issuance and a slow drift toward capital controls. He also reads the 2023 to 2025 gold rally as a regime warning, like the 1968 break of the London Gold Pool. A useful frame for anyone thinking about inflation protection. Tied to current events, so worth hearing soon.

picks.title: My Biggest Bet Isn't the Stock Market | Inside Meb Faber's Personal Portfolio
picks.match: Show Us Your Portfolio Meb Faber
picks.why: Cullen Roche walks Meb Faber through his own money. About a third of his net worth is in public markets, split between buy and hold (global stocks, bonds and real assets) and trend following, and the rest is his firm, farmland, his home and more than 400 startup bets. Faber makes the case for holding safe money in a diversified global portfolio instead of T-bills, which he estimates earns about 2 points more without deeper drawdowns, and explains why trend following gets half the public allocation after how it held up in 2008 and 2022. Roche adds that long-duration bonds stay risky even over long horizons. Evergreen.

picks.title: 2027 Tax Brackets Are Out (And 4 Retirement Numbers That Didn't Change)
picks.why: A short bonus episode on the IRS's 2027 inflation updates. Brackets and the standard deduction went up, but several thresholds that matter to retirees stayed frozen, so they quietly bite harder each year. It walks through how the new brackets change federal income tax, the income level where three key thresholds line up, and four frozen numbers that can raise a retiree's tax bill. Useful for year-end Roth conversion and withdrawal planning, so worth hearing before December.

picks.title: From Poker Pro to Elite Hedge Fund Manager: David Orr on Investing, Risk and AI
picks.match: Poker Pro to Elite Hedge Fund
picks.why: Jack Forehand talks with David Orr of Militia Capital about what professional poker taught him about probabilities and changing his mind, and why piling on more research often fails to improve a decision. He explains how he builds long and short theses while watching for exposures that several positions share, how AI has changed his research workflow, and why he worries about an oversupply of compute. They also cover opportunities in Japan and crowded shorts, and he closes with the case that broad index funds are the right answer for most individual investors. Mostly evergreen.

picks.title: Talk Your Book: The Anthropic IPO
picks.why: A Talk Your Book episode, so the guest's firm is a paying sponsor: Michael Batnick and Ben Carlson talk with Derek Yan of KraneShares about investing in public and private AI companies and how to build an AI allocation. The most useful part is the walk through what matters in Anthropic's S-1 filing, followed by the case that robotics is the next stage of AI. Listen with the sponsorship in mind. Tied to the IPO, so worth hearing soon.

picks.title: This Is The Problem With AI's Most Bullish Chart
picks.match: Problem With AI's Most Bullish Chart
picks.why: Stanley Lee of Liquid Compute argues that rising GPU rental rates partly reflect tightening credit, not just booming demand: lenders have cut loan-to-value from about 70% this summer to 50 to 60% now and are steering clear of newer neoclouds, and some are asking about put options on rental rates as a stand-in for Nvidia's backstop. Paul Kedrosky argues the buildout needs trillions in yearly revenue that only coding is close to delivering, calls Nvidia's customer financing circular, and says IPO oversubscription numbers mean little. Useful for anyone with AI-heavy index funds. Timely, so worth hearing soon.

picks.title: Who Pays for the AI Buildout? Two Bond Investors Take Us Inside the Debt Market
picks.match: Who Pays for the AI Buildout
picks.why: Two F/m Investments bond managers follow the AI money into credit. Wider spreads and pricier default swaps on big tech borrowers mean ordinary aggregate bond funds now carry more AI exposure than many holders realize, and if lenders balk, shareholders end up paying through new stock issuance. There is also a segment on short-duration TIPS and how rate risk can swamp inflation protection in a TIPS fund, something individual bonds held to maturity avoid. Timely, so worth hearing soon.

picks.title: Nvidia's 35% Drop and the Risk Retirees Aren't Paid to Take
picks.match: Nvidia s 35 Drop and the Risk Retirees
picks.why: Taylor Schulte argues that company-specific risk isn't reliably rewarded, and with Nvidia at about 6% of the S&P 500 it sits in every broad fund. Four popular funds covering about 4,000 companies still put roughly 40% in about 10 names. The Magnificent 7 were expected to grow earnings about 55% in 2026 yet gained about 3% through mid-November, versus 13% for the other 493. Some value indexes held stocks up 300% to 800% this year, so read the holdings, not the label. Evergreen with a timely hook.

picks.title: The Fed Is Hiking. Earnings Growth Is Slowing. Is This 2018 Again? | Barry Knapp
picks.why: Barry Knapp argues the Fed is hiking just as AI capex and earnings growth peak, which makes 2018 his closest analog, and warns of a possible 10% to 12% drop by year end; he is holding cash and has cut tech to about half of market weight. He sees trend inflation at 2.5% to 2.75% rather than 2%, calls inflation mostly a fiscal problem the Fed is misreading, notes the 10-year term premium is about 65 basis points versus about 125 before 2008, and ties a 50 basis point jump in 10-year TIPS yields to the AI capex peak. The counterpoint: he still sees roughly 12.5% trend earnings growth if capex spreads beyond AI. Timely, so worth hearing soon.

picks.title: How AI Is Forcing China to Reshape Industrial Policy
picks.why: Kyle Chan of Brookings explains how Beijing is adapting its industrial policy to the AI boom, where Chinese companies' goals clash with state plans, and how Huawei competes with Nvidia. The most useful thread for investors is why China's tech wins haven't turned into strong stock returns: a country or sector can win the technology race and still pay shareholders poorly. Timely, so worth hearing soon.

picks.title: The Three Poisons Behind the Sell-Off | Andy Constan on Why This Dip Is Different
picks.why: Andy Constan of Damped Spring argues this sell-off is not like the quick dips of the last five years, because three pressures are hitting at once: companies are spending cash on the AI buildout and issuing stock instead of buying it back, earnings expectations assume more AI-driven growth than the economy can deliver, and long-term rates are staying high instead of reversing. He uses the Kalecki-Levy profits framework to show why flat government deficits drag on corporate profits, reads new stock and bond deals that trade below their offer price as a sign of weaker demand, and explains how a long decline could hit spending through the wealth effect. He thinks the Fed is able but not willing to rescue stocks while inflation stays above target, and separates his long-term portfolio from tactical positions in stocks, bonds and gold, with nominal bonds as the hedge if this turns into a real slowdown. Timely, so worth hearing soon.

picks.title: What Jensen Huang's Stunning Return Means for the AI Trade
picks.why: Recorded after Nvidia's board brought Jensen Huang back and chip stocks jumped, with the S&P 500 already in a correction days after the Anthropic IPO. Alexander Altmann of Barclays reads the rally as a relief move rather than a fix, argues that AI's revenue and financing gaps outlast any change at the top of one company, and asks whether AI has become too big to fail for the market and the economy. Useful for anyone holding a total market fund, since so much of it now rides on the AI trade. Timely, so worth hearing soon.

picks.title: 'Just Buy an Index Fund' Worked for 40 Years. That May Be Changing
picks.why: Stephanie Guild, Robinhood's chief investment officer, argues that the tailwinds behind four decades of stock gains are fading. She leans on a Fed study crediting falling interest rates and corporate tax cuts with over 40% of profit growth from 1989 to 2019, sees retiring 401(k) savers turning from buyers into sellers, and points to AI power demand pushing up energy and food prices. A sober challenge to plans built on historical stock returns, best heard as a stress test rather than a reason to abandon indexing. Evergreen.

picks.title: Episode 100: Robin Wigglesworth
picks.why: Rick Ferri talks with Financial Times editor Robin Wigglesworth about his new history of how bonds built the modern world. The book treats leverage, not bonds themselves, as the core risk in past blowups, argues bond markets grew where governments were accountable and issuers had to compete for money, describes "constructive bubbles" that crash but leave railroads and housing behind, and explains why markets have grown more speculative since 1980. A good corrective for anyone who writes off nominal bonds. Evergreen.
